claims.text: The target eutectic high-entropy alloy has dual-phase lamellar colonies containing numerous internal boundaries.
Internal boundaries in the lamellar colonies serve as microcrack-initiation sites during room-temperature tensile deformation.
High-pressure and high-temperature treatment using a hexahedron-anvil apparatus will refine the dual-phase lamellar-colony structure.
The treatment will reduce microcrack-initiation sites at internal boundaries.
The post-processing treatment should be conducted at a temperature below the alloy melting point but high enough to promote controlled recrystallization.
An inert atmosphere will avoid oxidation during the treatment.
A suitable treatment duration can enable microstructural homogenization without coarsening.
Controlled homogenization, recrystallization, and stress redistribution will modify internal-boundary characteristics and reduce microcrack precursors.
High pressure compresses and diminishes defects at grain boundaries.
Elevated temperature promotes recrystallization and phase adjustments.
Pressure- and temperature-induced microstructural changes improve bonding between the two phases.
Improved interphase bonding and reduced boundary defects lower stress concentrations and suppress microcrack initiation during deformation.
The treated alloy will have higher room-temperature tensile strength than the conventionally processed baseline.
The treated alloy will have higher room-temperature strain-to-failure than the conventionally processed baseline.
The treated alloy will form fewer microcracks during room-temperature tensile testing than the conventionally processed baseline.
The intervention is expected to be effective primarily in eutectic high-entropy alloys with dual-phase lamellar morphologies.
The treatment benefits may not transfer to alloys with substantially different compositions or microstructures.
Pressure, temperature, and duration must be optimized separately for different alloy systems.
